newsitem.title: USA: FBI arrests Japanese man on high-tech fraud charge.
newsitem.headline: FBI arrests Japanese man on high-tech fraud charge.

text.p: The FBI said on Friday it had arrested a Japanese man accused of obtaining product information from a Silicon Valley firm by posing as a potential customer, when he worked for a competitor.
Masanori Uekihara, 41, was arrested on Wednesday at San Francisco International Airport after arriving from Japan, the FBI said.

He was arrested based on a federal complaint filed in U.S. District Court in San Jose in April 1996 charging him with wire fraud. Uekihara appeared before a U.S. Magistrate in San Francisco on Wednesday and was remanded to custody, the FBI said.

In an affidavit filed in support of the criminal complaint in April last year, FBI Special Agent Russell Atkinson said there was probable cause to believe that Uekihara falsely posed as an employee of Japanese electronics giant Toshiba Corp..
By doing so, he said, Uekihara obtained documents and computer chips from Maxim Integrated Products Inc., based in Sunnyvale, California.

According to a Maxim executive quoted in the affidavit, Uekihara, identifying himself as a Toshiba employee, visited Maxim's Sunnyvale offices in February 1996 and asked about literature for a Maxim product then under development -- an integrated circuit known as the MAX1630 used in regulating voltage on batteries in notebook computers.
Uekihara told Dave Timm, Maxim director of product development, he was looking for new technology to put into Toshiba products, the affidavit said.

Timm knew Toshiba was a market leader in notebook computers and was "a potentially huge customer for this chip," the affidavit said. Timm gave Uekihara the draft data sheet on the MAX1630 -- marked "confidential" -- and sent him chips in Japan in the belief that they were to be evaluated by Toshiba engineers, it said.

Soon afterwards, a Maxim employee in Japan saw a press report that Uekihara was employed by the Japanese subsidiary of Linear Technology Corp., a competitor to Maxim based in Milpitas, Calif. Toshiba told Maxim that Uekihara had worked for Toshiba but had left the company about six months earlier, the affidavit said.
Maxim sued Linear Technology in a California court in February 1996, accusing it of stealing product secrets, according to news reports.
A Linear Technology spokeswoman said Uekihara was employed by the company as area sales manager for Japan at the time of the incident but had since been dismissed.
She said his alleged actions were deceptive, but added that he acted on his own and "Linear in no way asked him or had him do it."
The spokeswoman said the information Uekihara allegedly obtained was already available to Maxim customers. She said Linear Technology and Maxim had settled the lawsuit.
A Maxim spokesman could not immediately be reached for comment.
If convicted of the wire fraud charge, Uekihara could be sentenced to up to five years in prison and fined a maximum of $1,000, the FBI said. Linear Technology does not face any criminal charges.
